\end{center}and assume matching is required to be monic. This requirement is often used in practice, because monic matching increases the expressiveness of DPO\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{habel2001doublerevisited}{}{}]}.
\par The approach in\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014}{}{}]} cannot prove $\rho$ terminating. For establishing termination (on all graphs), the weighted type graph $T$ has to contain a node with a loop (called a \emph{flower node}). The flower node ensures that every graph $G$ can be mapped into $T$. Then, in particular, the technique requires a weight decrease (from $L$ to $R$) for the case that the interface $K$ is mapped onto the flower node. However, this makes $L$ and $R$ indistinguishable for the technique in\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014}{}{}]}.
\par Although matches are required to be monic, the method of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]} overapproximates for unrestricted matches by design.
Observe that if matching is not monic, then graph $L$ of $\rho$, but with $x$ and $y$ identified, rewrites to itself, meaning $\rho$ is not terminating. As a consequence, the overapproximation of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]} causes it to fail in proving $\rho$ terminating for the monic matching setting. (For the same reason, the method of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]} fails on the simpler top span of Example\penalty\ \ref{example:fold:edge}, which is a DPO rule, for the monic matching setting.)
\par Rule $\rho$ can be proven terminating with our method as follows. Encode $\rho$ into PBPO${}^{+}${} using the standard encoding\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{overbeek2023quasitoposes}{}{}, Definition\penalty\ 71]}.). The resulting rule and a termination proof were given in Example\penalty\ \ref{example:dpo:as:pbpo} above.
\par Additional examples by Bruggink et al.\ that our method can prove are Example\penalty\ 4 of \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014}{}{}]} ($=$ Example\penalty\ 2 of \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]}), and Example 4 of \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]}. Additional examples that our method cannot prove are Example\penalty\ 1 and the example of Section\penalty\ 3.5 of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014}{}{}]}. However, unlike the earlier referenced Examples\penalty\ 5 and\penalty\ 6 of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]}, these examples are in reach if our morphism counting technique can take into account antipatterns (Remark\penalty\ \ref{remark:antipatterns} below), because they terminate because of local properties.
\par\begin{rem}A rule that matches an isolated node, and adds a loop, cannot be proven terminating with our method. For this, one must be able to count nodes \emph{without} loops (an \emph{antipattern}), which is currently unsupported. We believe that extending our method with support for such antipatterns is a natural first step for significantly strengthening it.
\end{rem}\par In \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{gwtg2024}{}{}]}, we generalize and strengthen the approach of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2015}{}{}]} to (a) be applicable in a wider range of categories and (b) be applicable when termination depends on matching restrictions. This enhanced weighted type graph technique can prove termination of Example\penalty\ \ref{example:DPO:rule:comparison}. However, it still fails for other systems which can be proven terminating by the approach presented in the current paper (for instance Example\penalty\ 6 of \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump2018modular}{}{}]}). Thus, even in settings where both methods are defined, the methods are strictly incomparable.
\par We discuss some additional related work.
An early systematic termination criterion for hypergraph rewriting with DPO, due to Plump, is based on the concept of forward closures\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump1995on}{}{}]}. Both of the examples proven terminating with forward closures, Example\penalty\ 3.8 (Example\penalty\ \ref{example:plump:string} above) and Example\penalty\ 4.1 of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump1995on}{}{}]}, can be handled with our method.
\par More recently, Plump formulated a modularity criterion for hypergraph rewriting using DPO\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump2018modular}{}{}]}: the union of two terminating systems is terminating if there are no sequential critical pairs. Of this paper, our method can prove three out of four examples: Examples\penalty\ 3 ($=$ Example 3.8 of\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump1995on}{}{}]}),\penalty\ 5 and\penalty\ 6. The modeling of Example 6 is Example\penalty\ \ref{ex:plump:jungle:eval:hypergraph} above.
Our method cannot prove Example\penalty\ 4 ($=$ the already discussed Example 5 of \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014}{}{}]}). It would be interesting to assess the strength of the modularity criterion (especially if generalized to PBPO${}^{+}${}) combined with our method.
\par Bruggink et al.\ have shown that string rewriting rules are terminating on graphs iff they are terminating on cycles\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014}{}{}]}, making cycle rewriting techniques\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{zantema2014termination, sabel2017termination}{}{}]} applicable to graph transformation systems consisting of string rewrite rules. Similarly, in another paper\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{overbeek2021from}{}{}]} we have shown that particular PBPO${}^{+}${} encodings of linear term rewrite rules are terminating on graphs iff they are terminating on terms.
\par There also exist a variety of approaches that generalize TRS methods (such as simplification orderings) to acyclic term graphs\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump1999term,plump97simplification,moser2016kruskal}{}{}]} and drags\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{dershowitz2019drags, dershowitz2023drag}{}{}]} (that possibly contain cycles)\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{dershowitz2018graph}{}{}]}.
\par\begin{rem}An interesting question is how the technique presented in this chapter relates to the many techniques available for term rewriting systems. Zantema\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{terese}{}{}, Chapter 6]} has roughly categorized the available termination techniques for TRSs as follows:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@syntactical methods, which inductively define a well-founded order directly on the terms;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@transformational methods, which define non-termination preserving transformations $\Phi$ on rewrite systems $(\Sigma,R)$, such that termination of $(\Sigma,R)$ can be proven by applying other techniques to $\Phi((\Sigma,R))$; and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@semantical methods, which interpret terms into some well-founded order using weight functions.
\end{itemize}One of the most well-known syntactical methods for TRSs is the recursive path order (RPO) by Dershowitz\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{dershowitz82orderings}{}{}]}. RPO has been adapted for acyclic term graphs and\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{plump1999term,plump97simplification,moser2016kruskal}{}{}]} and drags\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{dershowitz2018graph}{}{}]}.
\par Well-known transformational methods for TRSs include dependency pairs\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{arts2000termination}{}{}]} and semantic labeling\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{zantema1995termination}{}{}]}. As far as we know, no versions for graphs have been proposed.
\par For the semantical methods, finally, a fundamental result is that a TRS is terminating iff it admits a compatible well-founded monotone algebra\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{terese}{}{}, Theorem 6.2.2.]}. This of course also implies that finding such an algebra is hard. For TRSs, there exist well-known heuristics for finding polynomial interpretations\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{cherifa1987termination}{}{}]} and matrix interpretations\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{hofbauer2006termination, endrullis2006matrix}{}{}]}. The weighted type graph approach by Bruggink et al.\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{bruggink2014, bruggink2015}{}{}]}, discussed above, essentially corresponds to the matrix interpretation method.
\par Our weighted subgraph counting approach is distinctly semantical, but as far as we can see, it does not correspond directly to an existing method for term rewriting systems. Because an analogous approach would not exploit the inductive term structure, we also do not believe that it would be very powerful in the TRS setting.
\end{rem}\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Implementation}
\par We have implemented our termination method using Scala 3\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{odersky2021programming}{}{}]}. The software package is called {graphTT}\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{overbeek2024graphtt}{}{}]}, and it includes a REPL (read-eval print loop) for exploring relative termination proofs iteratively, where in each step detailed feedback about the proof process is provided (Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:repl}). Our algorithm is implemented generically for general categories, and one category is included (together with parsing methods for input files): ${\textbf{FinGraph}}$, the category of finite edge- and vertex-labeled directed multigraphs. After describing the REPL, we give a brief description of the implementation (Section\penalty\ \ref{sec:implementation:details}), which can be viewed as an example of computational (applied) category theory (see Remark\penalty\ \ref{rem:computational:applied:category:theory} below).
\par\begin{rem}\emph{Computational (applied) category theory}, initiated by Rydeheard and Burstall\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{rydeheard1988computational}{}{}]} in 1988, bridges the gap between programming and category theory. More specifically, Rydeheard and Burstall implemented a large body of category theory in ML.
For algebraic graph transformation in particular, Minas and Schneider\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{minas2010graph}{}{}]} proposed a Java implementation in 2010. In more recent years, Brown et al.\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{brown2023computationalJLAMP}{}{}]} have implemented algebraic graph rewriting in Julia, as part of the broader AlgebraicJulia\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{halter2020compositional, patterson2021categorical}{}{}]} applied category theory project.
The work by Brown et al.\ is especially interesting because the code is both general and performant.
\end{rem}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{REPL}
\par We describe the REPL used for exploring relative termination proofs by running through a simple example session.
\par When the REPL is invoked, it starts in system selection mode. One of the available commands is {help}, which shows the available commands. The output is as follows:

14.22636pt\hbox to330.77364pt{\lx@add@cssclass{ltx_verbatim}{#\ iso\ in\ R:\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ 0}\hss}\hss}\penalty\hbox to345.0pt{\kern 14.22636pt\hbox to330.77364pt{\lx@add@cssclass{ltx_verbatim}{#\ noniso\ in\ R:\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ 5}\hss}\hss}\penalty\hbox to345.0pt{\kern 14.22636pt\hbox to330.77364pt{\lx@add@cssclass{ltx_verbatim}{}\hss}\hss}\penalty\hbox to345.0pt{\kern 14.22636pt\hbox to330.77364pt{\lx@add@cssclass{ltx_verbatim}{>>\ The\ pruned\ system\ is\ empty!}\hss}\hss}\penalty\hbox to345.0pt{\kern 14.22636pt\hbox to330.77364pt{\lx@add@cssclass{ltx_verbatim}{>>\ You\ have\ proven\ system\ folding_an_edge\ terminating.}\hss}\hss}{\penalty}\hbox to345.0pt{\kern 14.22636pt\hbox to330.77364pt{\lx@add@cssclass{ltx_verbatim}{>>\ Returning\ to\ system\ selection\ mode.}\hss}\hss}\@endparenv As can be seen:
\begin{enumerate}\enumerate@item@a summary is given on the system level, indicating whether the sliding was successful for every rule, and partitioning the rules according to whether they are provably decreasing, provably nonincreasing (but not provably decreasing), or neither (i.e., possibly increasing);
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@a summary is given for every rule $\rho$ of the system, indicating, among others, the largest possible weight for $\Delta_{\rho}$ (Theorem\penalty\ \ref{thm:termination:by:element:counting}), and the weight of $R$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@for every rule $\rho$ and tile $T$, detailed data is given for the slide analysis. Here,
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@{morphisms into R'} indicates $|\mathrm{Hom}(T,R^{\prime})|$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@{of which valid} indicates $|S|$ for $S=\{t\in\mathrm{Hom}(T,R^{\prime})\mid\langle t\mid t_{R}\rangle\in{\mathcal{A}({\textbf{C}})}\}$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@{iso in R} indicates ${\mathrm{Hom}(T,R^{\prime})}_{\cong}^{t_{R}}\cap S$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@{noniso in R} indicates ${\mathrm{Hom}(T,R^{\prime})}_{\not\cong}^{t_{R}}\cap S$; and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@{ways to slide} indicates the number of possible slid tile sets into $L^{\prime}$. The number of choices for right inverses do not matter here: it is the number of outcomes.
\end{itemize}\end{enumerate}Moreover, the system is automatically pruned if possible. In this example the pruned system is empty, meaning the system is terminating. If the system is not empty, the process repeats, and the user can select a new set of tiles for the pruned system.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Implementation Details}
\par The implementation consists of seven packages, named {categorytheory}, {labeledgraph}, {parsing}, {repl}, {rewriting}, {termination}, and {util}. We comment on packages {categorytheory}, {labeledgraph}, {rewriting}, and {termination}.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsubsection}{toc}{Package \texttt{categorytheory}}
\par\par Package {categorytheory} contains general purpose categorical definitions, organized in a highly modular fashion. The library is designed to be reusable for other purposes. Some of the more complex definitions include the notions of a presheaf category and a topos.
\par Most of the definitions in package {categorytheory} are defined as \emph{traits}. A Scala trait can be described as a more powerful version of Java's \emph{interface}. A trait can take type parameters and define (abstract or implemented) members. It can also mix in other traits, which is Scala's way of implementing multiple inheritance. The definition of a topos is given in Listing\penalty\ \ref{code:topos}, for instance, where type parameters A} represent the collections of objects and arrows, respectively. All members of Quasitopos} trait, and three default implementations are provided. The code}

\par Package {labeledgraph} defines labeled graphs and graph homomorphisms as defined in Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:graph}. It also defines Topos} trait. Enumerations of homomorphisms are not naively implemented, but also not fully optimized. For our present purposes, this is sufficient.
\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Package \texttt{rewriting}}
\par Package {rewriting} contains, among others, the definitions of a PBPO${}^{+}${} rule and step. For computing the step, an immediate question is how morphism $u:K\to G_{K}$ is to obtained (Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:pbpostrong:rewrite:step}). The lemma below demonstrates a few things of interest:
\begin{enumerate}\enumerate@item@the pullback square ${t_{L}\circ l}={l^{\prime}\circ t_{K}}$ of the rewrite rule does not need to be used in the construction;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@the explicit construction of $u$ can be bypassed; and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@no search is needed (for universal morphisms or factorizations): (a) composition of morphisms, (b) construction of pullbacks, (c) construction of pushouts, and (d) verifying that a morphism is an isomorphism are the only required operations.
\end{enumerate}\par\begin{lem}Let a rule $\rho$ and morphism $\alpha:G_{L}\to L^{\prime}$ be given. By using the constructions outlined in the diagram:

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\end{equation}and by additionally verifying that $j$ is an isomorphism, the result of the PBPO${}^{+}${} rewrite step induced by $\alpha$ is computed.
Moreover, a PBPO${}^{+}${} rewrite step diagram as given in Definition\penalty\ \ref{def:pbpostrong:rewrite:step} can be reconstructed by defining the missing morphisms $m:L\to G_{L}$ and $u:K\to G_{K}$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@${m}={n\circ j^{-1}}$; and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@${u}={v\circ{{i}^{{-1}}}}$.
\end{itemize}\end{lem}\begin{proof}If $j$ is an isomorphism, it is easy to verify that $\alpha$ defines a strong match for match morphism ${m={n\circ j^{-1}}}:L\to G_{L}$. Moreover, morphism $i$ is known to be an isomorphism\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{overbeek2023quasitoposes}{}{}, Lemma 15]}. That the correct pushout is computed in the last step can then be observed as follows. First, using $\mathrm{PB}(3)$ we have $t_{K}={t_{K}\circ i\circ{{i}^{{-1}}}}={u^{\prime}\circ v\circ{{i}^{{-1}}}}$, which means that $v\circ{{i}^{{-1}}}$ is the unique $u:K\to G_{K}$ for which $t_{K}={u^{\prime}\circ u}$\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{overbeek2023quasitoposes}{}{}, Lemma 15]}. arbitrary category ${\textbf{C}}$, from Lemma\penalty\ \ref{lemma:computing:a:pbpoplus:step} it follows that the following conditions are sufficient for deciding whether ${A}\Rightarrow_{\mathrm{PBPO}^{+}}^{\rho}{B}$ for objects $A,B\in\mathrm{Ob}({\textbf{C}})$:
\begin{enumerate}\enumerate@item@for all $X,Y\in\mathrm{Ob}({\textbf{C}})$, the hom-set $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$ is finite; and
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\enumerate@item@pushouts, pullbacks, and morphism compositions are computable.
\end{enumerate}More specifically, one can use the construction given in Lemma\penalty\ \ref{lemma:computing:a:pbpoplus:step}, where the conditions ensure that
\begin{itemize}\itemize@item@all adherence morphism candidates $\alpha\in\mathrm{Hom}(A,L^{\prime})$ can be exhaustively considered;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@verifying whether a morphism $f:X\to Y$ is an isomorphism reduces to a finite search for a morphism $f^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)$ that satisfies ${f\circ f^{\prime}}=\mathrm{1}_{Y}$ and ${f^{\prime}\circ f}=\mathrm{1}_{X}$;
\par\vskip 4.0pt\vskip 4.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 1.0pt\itemize@item@verifying whether $B$ qualifies as a pushout object in PO(4) of Diagram\penalty\ \eqref{eq:computing:a:rewrite:step:diagram} reduces to a finite search for an isomorphism in $\mathrm{Hom}(G_{R},B)$.
\end{itemize}\par For the category of finite sets ${\textbf{FinSet}}$, the sufficient conditions hold. The same is true for functor categories $[I,{\textbf{FinSet}}]$ for which the index category $I$ is finite, which includes many graph categories of interest. This is because here the constructions are computed pointwise in ${\textbf{FinSet}}$.
\end{rem}\par\par\@@numbered@section{subsection}{toc}{Package \texttt{termination}}
\par Package {termination}, finally, contains the implementation of the termination method, currently implemented at the level of rm-adhesive quasitoposes. Listing\penalty\ \ref{code:termination} contains a code fragment that illustrates how the implementation utilizes the {categorytheory} library. When given a morphism
$f:T\to R^{\prime}$ (parameter {tiling}) rule $\rho$ (parameter {rule}), it computes set $\{l^{\prime}\circ\langle f\mid r^{\prime}\rangle\circ g\mid\text{$g$ is a right inverse for $\langle r^{\prime}\mid f\rangle$}\}$. Then, based on the selected counting class (either ${\mathrm{Hom}({\textbf{C}})}$, ${\mathrm{mono}({\textbf{C}})}$, or ${\mathrm{rm}({\textbf{C}})}$, represented by parameter {countingClass}), it verifies part of the conditions of Theorem\penalty\ \ref{thm:xi:is:injection}, also utilizing Proposition\penalty\ \ref{prop:preserving:a:factorization:and:factorization:systems}.

}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{o}}}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_space}{ }}{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{\textunderscore}}}).{\@listingGroup{ltx_lst_identifier}{{toSet}}}\@lst@endline}}{}}}\par\par\@@numbered@section{section}{toc}{Conclusion and Future Work}
\par We have introduced a termination method for graph transformation systems that can be utilized across frameworks, and which is defined in a broad array of categories. Our examples and comparisons with related work show that the method adds considerable value to the study of termination for graph transformation. We have also implemented the method in Scala, together with a REPL with which one can explore relative termination proofs iteratively.
\par Future work for strengthening the method includes solving the issues raised related to rule equivalence (Example\penalty\ \ref{example:dpo:as:pbpo}) and antipatterns (Remark\penalty\ \ref{remark:antipatterns}).
Methods for finding $\mathbb{T}$, if it exists, and identifying useful sufficient conditions for the non-existence of $\mathbb{T}$, would also be very useful. A possible metatheoretical direction for future research includes the question posed regarding PBPO${}^{+}${}-adhesivity{} (Remark\penalty\ \ref{remark:pbpo:adhesive:question}).
